query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), the retention or loss of toughness is governed by the degree of nanosegregation of principal elements (notably Ni, Cr, and Mn) at the grain boundaries. Excessive nanoclustering reduces grain-boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking, thereby lowering toughness, whereas controlling this segregation—either by optimized heat treatments or by introducing a small addition of Cr to form Cr-rich secondary phases that divert segregating elements away from the boundaries—preserves and enhances toughness. This effect is achieved by regulating the local chemical short-range order at the grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, face-centered cubic (fcc) HEA (for example, CrMnFeCoNi) with a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution and typical as-cast or minimally processed microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heat treatments with qualitatively different regimes to either accelerate or suppress grain-boundary nanosegregation. Optionally, introduce a small addition of Cr or another element that forms Cr-rich secondary phases to promote segregation away from the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing performed at room temperature and at intermediate elevated temperatures on samples with typical grain sizes processed via rapid solidification or conventional casting; the hypothesis is applicable for single-phase fcc HEAs under monotonic mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where the local concentration and clustering of elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) directly affect atomic bonding and cohesion.
generation.mechanism: When principal elements segregate excessively at grain boundaries, the local reduction in bonding strength leads to decohesion and facilitates crack initiation under stress. Conversely, by moderating the degree of nanosegregation or diverting segregating species into benign Cr-rich secondary phases, the grain-boundary cohesion is maintained, thereby retaining toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to conditions that promote increased nanosegregation will show reduced toughness, evidenced by more intergranular fracture features and lower fracture toughness values; in contrast, samples engineered to limit GB segregation (or to channel it into secondary phases) will exhibit higher toughness and more ductile, transgranular fracture morphologies compared to a baseline sample processed without such intervention.
generation.baseline: HEA samples processed under standard conditions with no deliberate modification of grain-boundary chemistry, expected to show moderate toughness and mixed fracture modes.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis applies to single-phase, chemically complex fcc HEAs with similar compositional and microstructural characteristics and may not directly translate to multiphase systems or ceramic-type high-entropy materials.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the extent of nanosegregation and reduction in toughness is not yet fully defined, and interactions with other factors (such as grain size, dislocation density, and processing history) may also be significant.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identically composed single-phase fcc HEAs with controlled variations in grain-boundary chemistry. Use differing heat treatments (e.g., rapid quenching versus prolonged annealing) and alloying strategies (with and without small additions of Cr to form secondary phases) to intentionally vary the degree of nanosegregation at grain boundaries. Conduct tensile tests and perform detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM and atom probe tomography) to quantify the extent of nanosegregation and correlate it with fracture toughness.
measurements: Fracture toughness and tensile ductility from mechanical tests
Fracture surface analysis (intergranular vs. transgranular features)
Quantitative measurements of grain-boundary segregation levels using APT or high-resolution TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in the degree of grain-boundary nanosegregation do not correlate consistently with changes in measured toughness—for example, if samples with higher segregation do not show significantly lower toughness or display intergranular fractures compared to the baseline—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.
